lesson.title: How Long Is It? Measuring Strings with len()
lesson.summary: The built-in len() function counts how many characters a string contains, and that count is essential for writing safe loops, validating input, and working with indices near the end of a string.
lesson.body:
Strings vary in length constantly. A name typed into a form might be four characters or forty, a line read from a file might be empty or might run past a hundred characters, and a program that wants to process that text correctly usually needs to know exactly how long it is before doing anything else. Python provides this through the built-in function len(), which takes a string as its argument and returns an integer: the exact number of characters it contains, including spaces and punctuation, since those count as characters too.

Calling len() is direct: len("PYTHON") returns 6, because the string has exactly six characters, P, Y, T, H, O, and N. This is the same number that defines the valid range of indices for that string, 0 through 5 for positive indices and -1 through -6 for negative ones, which is exactly why len() and indexing are so often used together. The last valid positive index of any string is always len(word) - 1, never len(word) itself, since counting starts at 0; trying word[len(word)] on "PYTHON" would attempt word[6], which raises an IndexError for the same reason word[6] always does on a six-character string.

len() becomes especially useful when combined with a loop, letting you visit every index of a string one at a time without hardcoding how many characters it has:

word = "PYTHON"
print(len(word))
for i in range(len(word)):
    print(word[i], end=" ")

The first print statement outputs 6. Then range(len(word)) becomes range(6), which produces the sequence of indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, exactly the valid indices for this string. The loop visits each in turn, printing word[i] followed by a space instead of a newline because of end=" ". The full output is P Y T H O N with a trailing space, one character at a time, built entirely from len() rather than a number typed by hand, so the exact same loop would work correctly no matter how long or short the string in word happened to be.

This is also the cleaner, safer alternative to the shortcut negative indexing offers. Earlier, word[-1] was shown to be equivalent to word[len(word) - 1], and seeing that equivalence spelled out with an actual len() call makes clear exactly why negative indexing works the way it does: it is performing that same length-based subtraction internally, just without asking you to write it out.

len() is not limited to strings; it works on lists, tuples, and other sequence types using the exact same idea of 'how many elements does this contain,' which is one more reason it is worth learning solidly here. A common and important habit is checking len(word) == 0 or the equivalent not word before processing a string, since an empty string, one with zero characters, is a completely valid string in Python and often needs to be handled as a special case before indexing into it, since word[0] on an empty string always raises an IndexError.
